title: SIADH with Severe Hyponatremia
sub: Small cell lung cancer · Medical oncology unit
profile: 72-year-old man with small-cell lung cancer, admitted with nausea, headache and new disorientation. At 12:00 sodium 118 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, glucose 104 mg/dL, measured serum osmolality 252 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg and urine sodium 52 mEq/L. Clinically euvolemic: no edema, orthostasis or pulmonary congestion. Renal function, thyroid testing and adrenal assessment do not suggest alternative causes; no diuretic use. Intake/output: 180 mL urine in 8 hours; weight 81.6 kg versus 79.5 kg three days ago. BP 158/92 mmHg, temperature 36.9°C; first chemotherapy cycle two weeks ago. The team diagnoses SIADH and orders an individualized 800 mL/day fluid limit with frequent neurologic/sodium checks. Duration of hyponatremia is uncertain; the protocol limits sodium increase to no more than 8 mEq/L in any 24 hours. Progressive neurologic symptoms require prompt hypertonic-saline evaluation rather than waiting for fluid restriction to fail.

Notes: Admission 08:00

Client reports nausea, poor appetite, fatigue and a dull headache for 3 days. Wife says he has been "mixed up" since last night and is passing very little urine. Confused to time and place. Lungs clear. No edema. Mucous membranes moist.
Home medications
No diuretics. Completed first chemotherapy cycle 2 weeks ago.
Vitals: BP 158/92 mm Hg · HR 84 · RR 18 · SpO₂ 96% on room air · T 36.9 °C (98.4 °F)
81.6 kg today · 79.5 kg at oncology clinic 3 days ago
Urine 180 mL in the past 8 hours
Labs: Serum Na⁺ 118 mEq/L · Serum osmolality 252 mOsm/L · K⁺ 3.6 mEq/L · Glucose 104 mg/dL · BUN 9 mg/dL · Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
Urine osmolality 480 mOsm/L · Urine Na⁺ 52 mEq/L
Orders: Fluid restriction 800 mL/24 h · Strict intake and output · Daily weight · Neurological checks every 2 hours · Serum sodium every 4 hours · Notify provider for Na⁺ < 115 mEq/L or any change in neurological status

items.stem: Tap the findings that specifically support symptomatic hypotonic hyponatremia with inappropriate antidiuresis in the displayed euvolemic client.
items.rationale: The neurologic symptoms, hypotonic hyponatremia and inappropriately concentrated urine support SIADH after the displayed alternative-cause assessment. SIADH is typically clinically euvolemic. Hypertension, weight gain or low output alone are not diagnostic hallmark criteria; normal glucose helps exclude a hyperglycemia-related sodium explanation.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.

blanks.pre: The serum osmolality of 252 mOsm/L shows
opts: hemodilution from too much water in the blood
blanks.answer: hemodilution from too much water in the blood

blanks.pre: while the urine osmolality of 480 mOsm/L shows
opts: urine that is concentrated despite a low sodium
blanks.answer: urine that is concentrated despite a low sodium

blanks.pre: and the urine sodium of 52 mEq/L reflects
opts: high sodium loss in the urine
the kidneys holding on to sodium
blanks.answer: high sodium loss in the urine

items.rationale: Hypotonic plasma should suppress antidiuresis and allow dilute urine. Persistently concentrated urine and urine sodium above 30 mEq/L in the displayed euvolemic context are compatible with SIADH after excluding other causes. Urine sodium alone neither proves renal salt wasting nor establishes the diagnosis. Measured osmolality is expressed in mOsm/kg.

items.stem: Which complication is the client at highest risk for right now?
options: Seizures and coma from brain swelling as the sodium falls
items.rationale: The book states that neurological changes are the most critical concern in SIADH. Falling sodium lets water move into brain cells, and late symptoms are confusion, seizures and coma. This client is already confused with a sodium of 118 mEq/L. The client has too much water, not too little, so hypovolemic shock does not fit. The potassium is normal, and skin breakdown is a longer-term risk.

items.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this client.
rows: Count ice chips and IV fluids toward the 800 mL limit
Encourage 2 L of oral fluids to relieve his headache
Offer hard candy or gum for thirst and dry mouth
Aim to bring the sodium back to 135 mEq/L within 12 hours
items.rationale: Count all fluids under the individualized 800 mL order and maintain seizure precautions. Oral care supports comfort without placing candy/gum in a confused client’s mouth before safety assessment. Unrestricted fluids worsen free-water retention. Follow the displayed protocol correction limit; a 17 mEq/L rise to 135 in 12 hours would be unsafe. The fluid limit is a specific order, not a universal SIADH volume.

items.stem: At 16:00 the sodium is 116 mEq/L and the client is drowsier. The provider prescribes 3% hypertonic saline. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Listen to lung sounds for crackles of pulmonary congestion
Increase the infusion rate if the next sodium has not risen
Keep the head of the bed flat or slightly elevated
Allow water as desired now that saline is infusing
Stop recording intake and output while the saline runs
items.rationale: Worsening drowsiness with sodium 116 requires prompt prescribed hypertonic treatment and close sodium/neurologic monitoring, not a prerequisite trial of failed restriction. Monitor respiratory status, maintain seizure precautions and position for airway/aspiration safety. Do not independently accelerate the infusion; follow the protocol correction limit and assess output for sudden aquaresis/overcorrection. Continue intake/output accounting and prescribed fluid management.

items.stem: The next morning the nurse reviews the client's progress. Which finding requires immediate follow-up with the provider?
options: Urine output 600 mL over the past 12 hours
Sodium 131 mEq/L this morning, up from 116 mEq/L at 16:00 yesterday
Oriented to person, place and time
items.rationale: A 15 mEq/L sodium increase in about 16 hours exceeds the displayed 8 mEq/L/24-hour protocol limit and requires immediate intervention assessment to prevent osmotic demyelination. Improved orientation does not make overcorrection safe. Increased urine output/weight loss may accompany aquaresis and should be interpreted with the sodium trajectory, not automatically accepted as reassuring. Correction limits depend on chronicity and ODS risk; this item specifies its protocol.

title: Addisonian (Adrenal) Crisis
sub: Gastroenteritis in known Addison disease · Emergency department
profile: 41-year-old woman with autoimmune Addison disease after 2 days of vomiting/diarrhea. She vomited her oral hydrocortisone doses and has no injectable rescue supply. Initial BP 76/44 mmHg, glucose 48 mg/dL, potassium 6.1 mEq/L, sodium 124 mEq/L, temperature 37.8°C. Chronic knuckle/elbow hyperpigmentation and salt craving. Emergency orders include IV hydrocortisone 100 mg followed by stress-dose therapy, isotonic-fluid resuscitation with reassessment, hypoglycemia treatment and repeat electrolytes/glucose under protocol. Continuous ECG monitoring and an urgent 12-lead ECG assess hyperkalemia; implement prescribed stabilization/shift/removal treatment when indicated concurrently with crisis treatment. Etiology of diarrhea is being investigated. Given the severe illness, the team has prescribed stool testing to investigate a possible infectious trigger; collection must not delay crisis resuscitation.

Notes: ED triage 14:10

Vomiting and watery diarrhea for 2 days; unable to keep her hydrocortisone tablets down since yesterday. Reports severe weakness, dizziness on standing and abdominal pain. Lethargic but answers questions. Skin dry with poor turgor. Darkened skin over the knuckles and elbows, which her husband says has been there for years. Says she has been craving salty foods.
History
Autoimmune Addison disease diagnosed 3 years ago. Home medication: oral hydrocortisone as prescribed.
Vitals: BP 76/44 mm Hg lying · HR 128 · RR 22 · SpO₂ 97% on room air · T 37.8 °C (100 °F)
Unable to stand for orthostatic readings: becomes faint on sitting up
Labs: Na⁺ 124 mEq/L · K⁺ 6.1 mEq/L · Glucose 48 mg/dL · BUN 41 mg/dL · Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL · Serum cortisol pending
Orders: Two large-bore IV lines · Hydrocortisone IV now (high dose, as prescribed) · D5NS bolus as prescribed, then reassess · Treat glucose < 70 mg/dL per hypoglycemia protocol · Electrolytes and point-of-care glucose every 1–2 hours · Stool culture · Continuous cardiac monitoring

items.stem: Which findings require immediate follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.
options: Darkened skin over the knuckles and elbows
items.rationale: The book lists the key features of an Addisonian crisis as severe hypotension, dehydration, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia and shock. A BP of 76/44, a glucose of 48, a potassium of 6.1 and a sodium of 124 all need action now. Darkened skin over the knuckles and salt craving are long-standing features of Addison disease, not signs of the acute crisis. A temperature of 37.8 °C is worth noting because infection can trigger crisis, but it is not the immediate threat.

items.stem: Which hormone imbalance best explains the client's sodium of 124 mEq/L and potassium of 6.1 mEq/L?
items.rationale: Aldosterone deficiency most directly explains combined sodium wasting and potassium retention in primary adrenal insufficiency. Cortisol deficiency also contributes to hypotension/hypoglycemia and may promote ADH-mediated hyponatremia; it is incorrect to say cortisol cannot affect sodium. SIADH alone does not account for this hyperkalemic primary-adrenal pattern; excess cortisol does not fit.

items.stem: Complete the diagram: the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

opts: Give high-dose IV hydrocortisone as prescribed
Start rapid IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline or D5NS

items.rationale: A client with Addison disease who could not take her hydrocortisone, with severe hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia and hyponatremia, is in an Addisonian crisis triggered by fluid loss and illness. The book's priority interventions are high-dose IV hydrocortisone and rapid IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline or D5NS, while monitoring electrolytes and blood glucose. Myxedema coma causes hypothermia and bradycardia; thyroid storm causes high fever and hypertension. Fluid restriction would deepen the shock, and levothyroxine and cooling treat thyroid emergencies.

items.stem: For each intervention, indicate whether it is anticipated or not anticipated for this client.
rows: Rapid infusion of normal saline or D5NS
Fluid restriction to 800 mL per day
Point-of-care glucose and electrolytes every 1–2 hours
Stool culture to look for the cause of the diarrhea
items.rationale: Give prescribed stress-dose IV hydrocortisone promptly, reassessed isotonic fluids and hypoglycemia treatment, with the ordered frequent glucose/electrolyte monitoring and urgent ECG-guided potassium assessment. Treat the underlying trigger. Collect the specifically ordered stool test without delaying resuscitation; not every short diarrheal illness requires culture. Fluid restriction and beta-blockade are inappropriate in this hypovolemic adrenal crisis.

items.stem: IV access is established, the D5NS bolus is running and the low glucose has been treated per protocol. Which prescription should the nurse carry out next?
options: Give her usual oral hydrocortisone dose with sips of water
Wait for the serum cortisol result before giving any steroid
Give a potassium binder before any other medication
items.rationale: Give stress-dose IV hydrocortisone promptly alongside fluid/glucose rescue; do not wait for cortisol results or substitute an inadequate usual oral dose during emesis/shock. Assess potassium urgently with ECG/continuous monitoring and implement indicated hyperkalemia treatment concurrently. A binder does not replace hormone rescue and is not a reason to delay it; potassium 6.1 must not simply be left untreated while waiting for fluids/steroids to work.

items.stem: Four hours later the nurse reassesses the client. Tap the findings that show the treatment is working.
items.rationale: The book says to monitor electrolytes and blood glucose in Addisonian crisis. A BP back to 104/66, a glucose of 96, a potassium of 4.8 and a sodium rising slowly to 127 all show the hydrocortisone and fluids are reversing the crisis. Darkened skin is a chronic sign that will not change in hours. Continued loose stools mean the trigger still needs treatment, and a urine output of 15 mL/h is still low and needs follow-up.

title: Acute Kidney Injury with Hyperkalemia
sub: Nephrotoxic drugs and contrast dye · Medical unit
profile: 70-year-old man admitted 5 days ago with pneumonia treated with IV gentamicin; contrast CT on day 2 and ibuprofen used for knee pain. Baseline creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, now 3.2 mg/dL; potassium 6.4 mEq/L, bicarbonate 16 mEq/L, muddy-brown granular casts on urinalysis. Urine output 220 mL/24 hours, weight 84.1 kg versus 81.5 kg, basal crackles, ankle edema and drowsiness/intermittent confusion. Temperature 36.8°C; knee pain 2/10. Bladder scan 40 mL; renal ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis. BP 132/78 mmHg, no preceding documented hypotensive episode. ECG shows peaked T waves with ventricular ectopy. Emergency team/nephrology orders include cardiac stabilization and potassium-shifting treatment with glucose monitoring, reassessment for definitive potassium removal/dialysis, review of nephrotoxins and individualized fluid/potassium management.

Notes: Client drowsy and intermittently confused overnight. Fine crackles at both lung bases. 2+ edema in both ankles. Says he is short of breath lying flat. Took ibuprofen at home most days for knee pain. Indwelling urinary catheter draining small amounts of dark yellow urine; bladder scan 40 mL. Pain 2/10 in the knees.
Medications
Gentamicin IV daily (day 5) · Ibuprofen 400 mg PRN (home medication continued on admission) · Contrast-enhanced CT chest on day 2
Vitals: BP 168/94 mm Hg · HR 92, occasional irregular beats · RR 24 · SpO₂ 93% on 2 L · T 36.8 °C (98.2 °F)
Urine 220 mL in the past 24 hours
Labs: K⁺ 6.4 mEq/L · BUN 68 mg/dL · Creatinine 3.6 mg/dL (1.0 on admission) · HCO₃⁻ 16 mEq/L · Na⁺ 133 mEq/L · Ca²⁺ 7.8 mg/dL
Muddy brown casts, renal tubular cells, protein 1+
Orders: Notify provider of K⁺ > 5.5 mEq/L · 12-lead ECG now · Calcium gluconate IV as prescribed · Regular insulin IV with dextrose as prescribed · Sodium polystyrene sulfonate as prescribed · Sodium bicarbonate as prescribed · Strict intake and output · Daily weight · Fluid restriction as prescribed · Continuous cardiac monitoring · Nephrology consult for possible dialysis

items.stem: Tap the findings in the record that are red-flag symptoms of acute kidney injury.
passage: Fine crackles at both lung bases
items.rationale: Very low urine output, acute weight gain, congestion and mental-status changes require urgent AKI/volume and metabolic assessment. A small bladder volume argues against bladder retention but does not independently exclude upper-tract obstruction; the displayed renal imaging contributes to that assessment. Confusion is nonspecific and requires evaluation rather than automatic attribution to uremia.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.
items.rationale: The creatinine rise, granular casts and medication exposures support intrinsic tubular injury as the most likely pattern. Gentamicin/NSAIDs are plausible contributors; contrast timing establishes association rather than proving causation, and infection/other causes are assessed. The small bladder scan and no-hydronephrosis imaging reduce obstruction concern. He is currently oliguric; AKI may be nonoliguric and does not invariably follow three fixed phases.

items.stem: Which complication poses the most immediate threat to this client's life?
options: Cardiac dysrhythmia from a potassium of 6.4 mEq/L
A new infection from the urinary catheter
Anemia from reduced red cell production
items.rationale: Potassium 6.4 with the displayed ECG changes/ectopy presents an immediate dysrhythmia risk requiring emergency protocol treatment and continuous monitoring. Long-term renal progression, infection and anemia do not outrank this active electrical threat. Dietary restriction alone is insufficient emergency treatment.

items.stem: Which interventions should the nurse anticipate in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the provider to stop the gentamicin and ibuprofen
Give a 1 L IV fluid bolus to flush the kidneys
Track intake, output and daily weights
Suggest a salt substitute to flavor his food
Encourage bananas and orange juice for energy
items.rationale: The book's AKI management is to treat the cause and stop nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides), track intake, output and daily weights, watch for fluid overload in the oliguric phase, restrict sodium and fluid based on status, and restrict potassium as needed. A large IV fluid bolus would add to the fluid overload he already has (crackles, edema, weight gain). Most salt substitutes are potassium chloride, and bananas and orange juice are high in potassium, so both would push his potassium of 6.4 higher.

items.stem: At 11:00 the nurse finds that no urine has drained into the catheter bag for 2 hours. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Request an extra dose of IV furosemide
Check the catheter and tubing for kinks or a blockage
Give a fluid challenge to test kidney response
Prepare the client for emergency dialysis
items.rationale: Check the catheter/tubing promptly for a reversible kink or obstruction while assessing the client and notifying the team of acute loss of output. This bedside check must not delay concurrent emergency hyperkalemia or respiratory treatment. Empiric extra diuretic or a fluid challenge without assessment can worsen this congested state; dialysis need is determined from the overall urgent clinical picture.

items.stem: The next morning the nurse reviews the client's response to treatment. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or a need for further action.
rows: More difficult to rouse than yesterday
Crackles now heard to the middle of both lungs
items.rationale: The lower potassium and improved bicarbonate are favorable observed trends; do not infer that an undocumented specific binder or bicarbonate dose caused them. Worsening consciousness and spreading crackles require urgent evaluation for metabolic/respiratory deterioration and dialysis indications. A lower weight is a favorable individual fluid trend but does not override worsening lung findings. Acute hyperkalemia needs stabilization/shift/removal and serial reassessment; SPS is not rapid definitive rescue.

title: Increased Intracranial Pressure
sub: Traumatic brain injury · Neuro intensive care unit
profile: 34-year-old man with traumatic brain injury after a motorcycle crash, with an ICP monitor. At 00:00 GCS 15, pupils equal/reactive 3 mm and ICP 12 mmHg. At 02:00 GCS 13, worsening headache, forceful emesis, right pupil 5 mm/sluggish and ICP 24 mmHg sustained despite initial measures. BP 134/78 mmHg, temperature 37.3°C, SpO₂ 97% on 2 L/min, glucose 118 mg/dL. Bed is flat with a pillow flexing the hips. Neurosurgery is notified urgently. Ordered plan: maintain prescribed cerebral perfusion goal, elevate head 30° with midline neutral alignment if hemodynamically tolerated, and give IV mannitol after volume/renal assessment. Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, no hypovolemia; track sodium/osmolality and output. Report ICP above 20 mmHg under the specific notification order; treatment decisions incorporate sustained values above 22 mmHg and neurologic/perfusion findings.

Notes: Alert, oriented × 3, follows commands. GCS 15. Pupils 3 mm, equal and brisk. Reports mild headache. Sutured scalp laceration.

Difficult to rouse, opens eyes to voice, oriented to person only. GCS 13. Reports worsening headache. Vomited forcefully twice without nausea beforehand. Right pupil 5 mm and sluggish, left 3 mm and brisk. Found lying flat with head turned to the left and a pillow under his knees.
Vitals: BP 128/78 mm Hg · HR 82 · RR 16 regular · SpO₂ 98% on 2 L · T 37.1 °C · ICP 12 mm Hg
BP 142/80 mm Hg · HR 76 · RR 18 regular · SpO₂ 97% on 2 L · T 37.3 °C · ICP 24 mm Hg
Labs: Na⁺ 139 mEq/L · Glucose 118 mg/dL · Hgb 13.1 g/dL · Platelets 210,000/mm³
CT head on admission: right frontal contusion with surrounding swelling
Orders: Neurological checks and pupils every hour · Head of bed 30 degrees · ICP monitoring; notify for ICP > 20 mm Hg · Mannitol IV as prescribed for ICP > 20 mm Hg · Stool softener daily · Suction as needed

items.stem: Which findings at 02:00 indicate that the client's intracranial pressure is rising? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: The book's early signs of increased ICP are a decreased level of consciousness, headache, pupil changes (sluggish, unequal) and nausea or vomiting that is often projectile. The ICP of 24 mm Hg is above the normal 5–15 mm Hg. The temperature, oxygen saturation and glucose are within acceptable limits and do not reflect pressure inside the skull.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.

blanks.pre: The first critical sign of worsening ICP is
opts: a drop in level of consciousness
blanks.answer: a drop in level of consciousness

blanks.pre: sign made up of a widened pulse pressure, irregular respirations and

items.rationale: A falling level of consciousness is a common early warning sign, but neurologic findings do not follow an invariable sequence. Cushing’s response—hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular respirations—is a late, ominous pattern. Any new pupil change, posturing or declining consciousness warrants urgent evaluation; do not wait for the complete triad.

items.stem: Complete the diagram: the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

opts: Lay the client flat to improve blood flow to the brain
Elevate the head of the bed 30 degrees with the head midline
Suction for 30 seconds to clear the airway fully
Bend the hips with pillows under the knees for comfort

items.rationale: The displayed neurologic/ICP deterioration supports increased intracranial pressure. Use the prescribed head alignment/elevation while maintaining cerebral perfusion, and give the specifically ordered mannitol after the displayed renal/volume assessment. Mannitol is not mandatory for every ICP elevation. Follow consciousness/pupils closely; avoid prolonged unnecessary suction, straining and positions that impair venous drainage. Airway suction is limited to clinically necessary brief passes under protocol.

items.stem: For each nursing action, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated for this client.
rows: Keep the head midline and neutral
Keep a pillow under the knees to flex the hips
Limit each suction pass to 10–15 seconds
Encourage him to bear down to move his bowels
Trend ICP readings and report values above 20 mm Hg
Keep the bed flat to lower blood pressure in the head
items.rationale: The ordered notification trigger is 20 mmHg; severe-TBI guidance uses sustained ICP above 22 mmHg as an initial treatment threshold interpreted with the clinical picture. This symptomatic 24 mmHg reading needs urgent action. Maintain head alignment/elevation and cerebral perfusion, avoid straining/hip flexion and perform only necessary brief suction under protocol. Bed-flat positioning is not ordered to treat this ICP rise.

items.stem: Emergency neurosurgical assistance has already been activated. The airway is patent and oxygenation is maintained. Which ordered bedside actions follow a logical intervention-and-reassessment sequence?
steps: Check the airway and oxygen saturation
Raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees, center the head and remove the knee pillow
Recheck level of consciousness, pupils and ICP
items.rationale: The stem establishes that emergency escalation occurred. Confirm rescue essentials, correct the observed position while maintaining perfusion, give specifically prescribed osmotherapy after required safety assessment and assess its response. Continuous monitoring accompanies all steps; the item does not require withholding repeated assessments until the end.

items.stem: At 04:00 the nurse reassesses the client. Tap the findings that show the intracranial pressure is still rising.
passage: Urine output 350 mL in the past hour
items.rationale: New widened pulse pressure/bradycardia, irregular respirations, fixed enlarged pupil and posturing are ominous neurologic deterioration requiring immediate rescue. Urine output 350 mL/h is not a specific sign of rising ICP, but after osmotherapy it still requires fluid, electrolyte/osmolality and medication-effect assessment; do not dismiss it as harmless. Acceptable SpO₂ and temperature do not negate the neurologic emergency.

title: Myasthenic Crisis
sub: Missed pyridostigmine doses during a viral illness · Emergency department
profile: 38-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis after a week of respiratory illness, now severe respiratory/bulbar weakness. Two pyridostigmine doses were missed because swallowing worsened; infection is an additional suspected trigger. At arrival SpO₂ 86% on room air, weak cough, pooled secretions/drooling, reduced basal breath sounds, bilateral ptosis/diplopia and facial weakness; alert/oriented, HR 112/min. ABG pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 58 mmHg. Neurology and expert airway team are activated, with serial respiratory-strength assessment as feasible without delaying ventilation. Plasma exchange is prescribed. Neurology directs pyridostigmine use during intubation/recovery, considering secretion burden.

Notes: ED triage 09:20

Has had a cold for a week. Missed her last two pyridostigmine doses because she could not swallow the tablets. Speaks in short phrases, with a weak, nasal voice. Drooping of both eyelids and double vision (her usual symptoms), now much worse. Cannot swallow her own saliva and is drooling. Weak cough. Breath sounds decreased at both bases. Masklike facial expression. Alert and oriented. Very anxious: "I can't get enough air."
Bowel
Last bowel movement yesterday, formed. No abdominal cramping.
Vitals: BP 136/84 mm Hg · HR 112 · RR 30, shallow · SpO₂ 86% on room air · T 37.6 °C (99.7 °F)
Unable to count past 8 in one breath
Labs: ABG: pH 7.31 · PaCO₂ 52 mm Hg · PaO₂ 58 mm Hg · HCO₃⁻ 25 mEq/L
WBC 11,200/mm³ · Na⁺ 138 mEq/L · K⁺ 4.0 mEq/L · Chest x-ray pending
Orders: Oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92% · Continuous pulse oximetry · Respiratory therapy and anesthesia to bedside; prepare for intubation · Nothing by mouth · Pyridostigmine as prescribed (route per provider) · Neurology consult for plasmapheresis · Lorazepam IV as needed for anxiety · Morphine IV as needed for dyspnea · Cyclobenzaprine as needed for neck muscle aches

items.stem: Tap the findings in the record that require immediate follow-up by the nurse.
passage: Cannot swallow her own saliva and is drooling
Breath sounds decreased at both bases
items.rationale: Inability to manage secretions, weak cough and inadequate ventilation threaten airway protection and breathing. The displayed hypoxemia is already severe, but desaturation/hypercapnia may be late; do not await them before acting on bulbar/respiratory weakness. Ptosis/diplopia/facial weakness need assessment but are less immediate than this respiratory crisis; preserved orientation does not ensure adequate ventilation.

items.stem: Which explanation best fits the client's findings?
options: Cholinergic crisis from too much pyridostigmine
Myasthenic crisis from too little pyridostigmine
New Guillain-Barré syndrome after a viral infection
items.rationale: Known MG with progressive respiratory/bulbar weakness during infection supports myasthenic crisis. Missed doses may contribute but are not its universal cause. Evaluate medication toxicity and other causes clinically; absence of diarrhea alone does not prove the diagnosis. Anxiety cannot account for the displayed respiratory-muscle failure/hypercapnia.

items.stem: Complete the diagram: the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

opts: Support the airway and prepare for assisted ventilation
Give an extra pyridostigmine tablet by mouth now
Prepare the client for plasmapheresis as prescribed
Give IV lorazepam to ease her breathing
Respiratory status: SpO₂, rate and effort
Ability to swallow and clear secretions

items.rationale: Provide airway/ventilation support and prepare the prescribed plasma exchange while following respiratory strength, effort and secretion/swallowing function. Giving an extra oral tablet to this unsafe-swallowing client risks aspiration; sedative treatment for anxiety may worsen ventilatory failure. Atropine is not treatment for myasthenic muscle weakness. Crisis treatment and cholinesterase-medication decisions are directed by neurology.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the admission orders. Which prescriptions should the nurse clarify with the provider before giving? Select all that apply.
options: Oxygen to keep SpO₂ at or above 92%
Lorazepam IV as needed for anxiety
Morphine IV as needed for dyspnea
items.rationale: Clarify nonessential lorazepam, morphine for dyspnea and muscle-relaxant orders during active ventilatory weakness because of sedation/respiratory risk. Oxygen, monitoring and NPO support rescue but do not replace ventilation. Neurology may hold pyridostigmine during intubation because of secretions and restart it during recovery; do not automatically continue/increase it as the sole crisis treatment.

items.stem: While waiting for the anesthesia team, the client begins to gurgle and cannot clear her secretions. Her SpO₂ is 84%. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Give her pyridostigmine tablet with a sip of water
Sit her upright and suction her mouth and throat
Prepare her for a Tensilon (edrophonium) test
Give the prescribed lorazepam to slow her breathing
items.rationale: Sitting upright and immediately suctioning pooled oral/pharyngeal secretions addresses the displayed airway obstruction while expert ventilation/intubation support is mobilized. Give oxygen and assist ventilation as clinically necessary after clearing the airway. Oral medication risks aspiration; diagnostic testing must not delay airway rescue, and an anxiolytic can worsen ventilatory weakness.

items.stem: After intubation and plasma exchange, neurology restarts/titrates pyridostigmine as respiratory strength improves. Over 48 hours, which individual findings indicate improvement or need follow-up?
rows: Stronger hand grip and a forceful cough
Three watery stools since the last dose
items.rationale: Stronger grip/cough, adequate post-extubation oxygenation and a documented safe-swallowing plan are favorable. New diarrhea and HR 52 may reflect cholinergic adverse effects or another cause and require urgent prescriber/medication assessment; they alone do not prove full cholinergic crisis. Atropine treats selected muscarinic effects, not neuromuscular weakness. No cough with small sips alone cannot exclude silent aspiration.

title: Sickle Cell Vaso-Occlusive Crisis
sub: Dehydration after intense exercise · Emergency department
profile: 19-year-old man with HbSS disease after prolonged soccer practice in heat; pain 9/10. Stable outpatient hemoglobin baseline 7.4–7.8 g/dL; today 7.6 g/dL with reticulocyte count similar to baseline, no new jaundice/dark urine or splenic enlargement. Temperature 38.3°C, SpO₂ 92% on room air, HR 118/min, BP 128/76 mmHg, dry mucosa and urine specific gravity 1.030; alert/oriented. Prescribed plan includes prompt IV opioid analgesia, reassessed hydration and oxygen for the displayed hypoxemia. Fever/hypoxemia prompt urgent infection and acute-chest-syndrome assessment, cultures/imaging/antibiotics as indicated; uncomplicated pain crisis is not assumed. Takes daily hydroxyurea.

Notes: ED triage 18:30

Severe aching pain in the lower back, both thighs and knees that began 4 hours after a 3-hour practice. Drank little water. Rates pain 9/10. Reports feeling very tired. Mucous membranes dry. No jaundice. Alert and oriented. Spleen not palpable. Lungs clear; denies chest pain or cough. Says, "This is like my usual crises, just worse." Took ibuprofen at home without relief.
History
Sickle cell disease since infancy. Takes hydroxyurea daily. Last crisis 8 months ago. Baseline hemoglobin about 8 g/dL.
Vitals: BP 128/76 mm Hg · HR 118 · RR 22 · SpO₂ 92% on room air · T 38.3 °C (100.9 °F)
Labs: Hgb 7.6 g/dL · WBC 15,400/mm³ · Platelets 480,000/mm³ · Reticulocytes 9% · Urine specific gravity 1.030
Orders: Oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥ 95% · IV 0.9% sodium chloride as prescribed · Morphine IV as prescribed for pain, reassess after each dose · Chest x-ray · Blood and urine cultures · Antibiotics as prescribed if infection suspected · Pain reassessment every hour

items.stem: Which findings require follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.
options: Urine specific gravity 1.030 with dry mucous membranes
items.rationale: Severe pain, fever, hypoxemia, dehydration and tachycardia require prompt assessment/treatment. Fever and low saturation warrant evaluation for infection/acute chest syndrome rather than attributing everything to vaso-occlusion. Hemoglobin is within this client’s explicitly displayed stable baseline; a generic low population range would not establish safety. Monitor individual anemia and perfusion trends.

items.stem: Complete the sentences.

blanks.pre: This crisis was most likely triggered by

opts: sickle and block small blood vessels
swell and burst in the spleen
clump with platelets in large arteries
blanks.answer: sickle and block small blood vessels

items.rationale: Dehydration/intense exercise are plausible triggers for vaso-occlusion in this HbSS client. He inherited two HbS alleles; sickle cell disease also includes compound genotypes such as HbSC and HbS/beta-thalassemia. Deoxygenated HbS polymerization produces rigid cells and microvascular obstruction. Hydroxyurea raises protective fetal hemoglobin and reduces episodes; it is not the trigger being tested.

items.stem: Which type of sickle cell crisis is the client most likely experiencing?
items.rationale: Severe pain after dehydration is most consistent with vaso-occlusive pain. The displayed baseline hemoglobin/reticulocytes and absence of new splenic enlargement or hemolysis signs make the competing crises less likely. Fever/hypoxemia still require urgent evaluation for infection and acute chest syndrome; the pain diagnosis does not exclude concurrent complications.

items.stem: For each intervention, mark whether it is appropriate under this client’s prescribed acute pain plan or not appropriate under that plan.
rows: Give the prescribed IV analgesic within 30 minutes of arrival
Give aspirin for the fever and pain
Hold pain medication until the blood count results
Offer guided imagery and distraction along with medication
items.rationale: Provide prompt prescribed analgesia, individualized hydration, oxygen for hypoxemia and supportive nonpharmacologic measures. The institution’s 30-minute analgesia target is reasonable and should not be delayed for laboratory results. Do not substitute unprescribed aspirin for the individualized regimen. Therapeutic aspirin is not universally contraindicated in SCD because it inevitably causes acidosis; salicylate toxicity is a distinct risk. Evaluate fever and oxygenation urgently.

items.stem: The IV line is in and the prescribed fluids are running. Put the nurse's next actions in order. Tap each in sequence; tap again to undo.
steps: Reassess pain, sedation level and respiratory rate after the dose
Give the next prescribed analgesic dose if pain is still severe at reassessment
items.rationale: Breathing comes first: his SpO₂ is 92% and low oxygen promotes more sickling, and applying oxygen takes seconds. The book then calls for analgesia within 30 minutes, so the prescribed IV morphine is given next. Pain, sedation and breathing are reassessed after the dose to judge whether it worked and whether it is safe to give more. Only then is the next prescribed dose given if the pain is still severe.

items.stem: Before discharge, the nurse reviews home care with the client. Which statements show the teaching was effective? Select all that apply.
options: "I'll drink fluids steadily all day, especially at practice."
"I can take aspirin at home if my joints start to hurt."
"Getting dehydrated, getting sick or being stressed can set off a crisis."
"I only need to push fluids once the pain starts."
"Hydroxyurea raises my fetal hemoglobin, which cuts down sickling and pain."
"I can stop hydroxyurea when I feel well."
items.rationale: Consistent individualized hydration, trigger awareness and continued prescribed hydroxyurea support prevention. Follow the personal pain plan and discuss new OTC medicines with the team; drug risks depend on the medication and clinical context rather than a blanket aspirin/acidosis rule. Drinking only after pain begins and stopping preventive therapy when well undermine prevention. Include urgent follow-up for fever or respiratory symptoms in discharge teaching.
